image.subject: Sergey Brin: a young man in his late twenties with curly dark hair and a casual open shirt, animated expression, leaning back with arms folded in a cluttered Google office in 2001, a whiteboard of equations behind him

storyboard.claim: The Google founders came from academia and see middle management as pure friction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brin leaning back, arms folded, in a cluttered 2001 startup office with equations on the whiteboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Google founders scene after the disdain-for-management setup.
storyboard.addedInformation: The founders' attitude toward corporate structure is visible in his posture.

image.subject: an engineer at a workstation with two monitors and a code editor, a thick stack of printed status reports and a meeting agenda pushed to the far corner of the desk, the engineer's hand hovering over the keyboard

storyboard.claim: Non-technical staff slow brilliant engineers with status updates and bureaucracy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An engineer's desk crowded by status reports while the keyboard waits unused.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the founders saw managers as friction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the concrete cost of status reporting to engineers.

storyboard.claim: The founders called their plan a disorg, firing the engineering managers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold statement text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the experiment the previous beat set up.
storyboard.addedInformation: The name itself, disorg, is the founders' own term.

image.subject: an empty glass-walled Silicon Valley office with a long conference table and whiteboards, every chair pushed in, late afternoon light across the floor

storyboard.claim: All engineering managers were removed; everyone reported directly to an engineering VP.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty glass office with a long table and no one seated.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the firing of the engineering managers.
storyboard.addedInformation: The room is empty, showing the managers are gone.

image.subject: an open-plan room of engineers' desks with no walls or partitions between them, each desk with a laptop and loose papers, people talking across the aisles

storyboard.claim: The founders believed free-flowing academic structures foster the most disruptive innovation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wide open-plan room with no partitions and engineers talking across desks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the founders' theory behind the disorg.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows what a flat, unwalled structure looks like in practice.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, walking beside Larry Page: a young man in his late twenties with tousled brown hair and a casual sweater, thoughtful expression, down a bright Google office corridor

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell walks the halls with Larry Page, debating the flat structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell and Page side by side in a corridor, deep in conversation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces Bill Campbell into the Google office scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Campbell's direct conversational style with the founder.

image.subject: a crowded engineering room with desks piled with paper and cables, two monitors per desk, a whiteboard covered in crossed-out arrows and reporting lines

storyboard.claim: The company starts to feel the chaos of the flat structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A cluttered engineering room with a whiteboard of crossed-out reporting lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Campbell's debate shifts to the consequences of the flat structure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The whiteboard shows the reporting lines that were removed.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning in beside an engineer's desk with two monitors and a code editor, the engineer turning from his screen to look up

storyboard.claim: Campbell stops a software engineer in the middle of writing code and interrupts him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell leaning into an engineer's desk while the engineer turns away from the code.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the chaos to a concrete moment with one engineer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Campbell's direct, unannounced way of starting a conversation.

storyboard.claim: Campbell asks the engineer point blank whether he wants a manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The question stands alone as text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Campbell's question to the engineer from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The surprising question is the point, so the text carries it.

image.subject: an engineer's desk with two monitors and a code editor, the engineer's hand resting on the keyboard as he turns to face the camera, a half-written function on the screen

storyboard.claim: The engineer says yes, he wants a manager, for reasons people would not expect.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The engineer's desk and screen as he gives his answer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The unfinished code shows the answer interrupted real work.

storyboard.claim: The engineer wants someone to break technical ties and to learn.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two short items in a list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the reasons behind the engineer's yes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the two specific things he asks of a manager.

image.subject: a whiteboard covered in a network diagram of circles linked by lines, one circle at the center connected to every other circle, drawn in blue marker

storyboard.claim: A manager is a network hub that connects the employees who generate the data.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard network with one hub connected to many nodes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The engineer's answer reframes the manager's role.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram makes the network idea visible.

image.subject: A manager: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, pulling a stack of printed reports toward her side of the desk

storyboard.claim: The old-school manager hoards the data and takes the credit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pulling reports to her side of the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the old boss with the network view.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reports on her side show hoarding.

storyboard.claim: The engineer says he needs a router, not a boss.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The quoted line as text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The engineer's line rejects the old boss idea.
storyboard.addedInformation: The router metaphor is his own phrasing.

storyboard.claim: A title means nothing unless it operationalizes excellence for the people below.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Draws the takeaway from the router metaphor.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the test for a manager's title.

image.subject: a manager's desk on a Monday morning, a calendar and a planner open beside a laptop, a coffee cup, the chair pushed back from the desk

storyboard.claim: The Disorg highlights a misunderstanding about what a manager does on Monday morning.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A desk with a planner and a coffee cup on a Monday.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the router idea to the practical day-to-day job.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the lesson to an ordinary workday.

image.subject: A manager: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, standing behind a seated engineer and looking over his shoulder at the code on his screen, one hand on the back of his chair

storyboard.claim: A manager should not stand over someone's shoulder and micromanage the work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager looming over a seated engineer's shoulder.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the manager's job is not.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the micromanagement posture being rejected.

image.subject: Eric Schmidt: a man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, seated at a glass-walled conference table, leaning in to a small group of papers, clearing a path

storyboard.claim: The job is to break ties, resolve conflicts, and remove roadblocks for people doing the work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Schmidt at a conference table, attentive, clearing obstacles from the papers in front of him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the real job after the micromanage contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the attentive, facilitating posture of the manager.

image.subject: an empty corner office with a high-backed leather chair behind a large desk, a single closed folder on the desk, the chair turned to face the window

storyboard.claim: A manager who does not facilitate is just enforcing hierarchy for his own ego.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A large empty executive chair behind a big desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the argument about facilitation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The empty throne-like chair stands for the ego hierarchy.

storyboard.claim: The sources give a concrete example of Bill Campbell learning this lesson.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions into the Donna Dubinsky story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Signals the story that follows.

storyboard.claim: Campbell did not preach this from day one; he had to be confronted with it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the Donna Dubinsky story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Says the lesson was learned under pressure, not taught.

image.subject: a 1990s software company office with beige desktop computers and paper binders, a ClariS box on a shelf, a wall calendar showing the year 1991

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell was CEO of ClariS, a software spin-off from Apple.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A 1990s office with beige computers and a ClariS box on the shelf.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the setting of the Donna Dubinsky story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dates the story to the early 1990s software era.

image.subject: a row of football trophies on a shelf in a 1990s office, a beige computer on the desk beside them, a half-open window letting in afternoon light

storyboard.claim: Campbell came off major successes at Apple and felt huge pressure to make ClariS a hit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Football trophies and a beige computer in a 1990s office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the pressure on Campbell at ClariS.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trophies show his football past and past wins.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning over a desk covered in printed spreadsheets, one finger pointing at a line

storyboard.claim: Campbell became detail-oriented and acted as a dictatorial manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell pointing at a spreadsheet, looming over the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes Campbell's behavior at ClariS.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the granular control in his posture.

image.subject: A manager: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, reaching over to take the keyboard from the colleague's hands

storyboard.claim: You get promoted for being good at the work, then try to do everyone's work as manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reaching for a colleague's keyboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why detail-oriented managers fall into the trap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the manager taking over someone else's work.

image.subject: an office door in a late-afternoon 1990s corridor swinging shut, a glass pane showing the dim silhouette of a seated man at a desk inside

storyboard.claim: Donna Dubinsky walks into Bill's office late one afternoon and closes the door.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A door swinging shut on a corridor, a seated silhouette behind the glass.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the Dubinsky confrontation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The closed door signals a serious private talk.

storyboard.claim: Dubinsky tells him to his face that if he keeps telling everyone what to do, they will all quit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the confrontation behind the closed door.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the quoted warning that follows.

storyboard.claim: Your title makes you a manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The quoted line as text.
storyboard.onScreenText: YOUR TITLE MAKES YOU A MANAGER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the first half of the warning.
storyboard.addedInformation: The line that splits title from leadership.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, looking at his own reflection in a dark office window, quietly taking in the words

storyboard.claim: Your people make you a leader; it struck a massive chord with Campbell.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell reflected in a window, absorbing the words.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the second half of Dubinsky's warning.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reflection shows him taking the lesson personally.

image.subject: a printed org chart pinned to a corkboard in a Silicon Valley office, one box crossed out in red marker, a few sticky notes of names pinned around it

storyboard.claim: Authority is not granted by an org chart HR prints out; it is granted by the team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A pinned org chart with one box crossed out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the warning to the principle it reveals.
storyboard.addedInformation: The crossed-out box shows that the chart does not confer authority.

image.subject: a glass office door opening onto a corridor, a laptop bag over one shoulder as a team member walks out with an empty cardboard box in hand

storyboard.claim: A dictator loses the most talented people, who have options in the job market.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team member leaving through a glass door with a box.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the consequence of dictatorial management.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the departure in concrete terms.

storyboard.claim: A manager's authority emerges by establishing credibility by making subordinates' lives easier.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the positive rule after the warning.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines where authority actually comes from.

storyboard.claim: Didn't Larry Page have a valid point about the Disorg?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The question stands alone as text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host pushes back on the credibility lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: Opens the counter-argument.

storyboard.claim: In pure creative fields, academic models without bosses foster innovation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates Page's argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the argument as a claim about creative fields.

image.subject: an empty university lecture hall with rows of wooden seats and a chalkboard covered in diagrams, no instructor in sight

storyboard.claim: Academic models without strict bosses usually foster the most disruptive innovation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty lecture hall with rows of seats and a chalkboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the academic example behind Page's view.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lecture hall stands for the academic model.

storyboard.claim: Does inserting a management layer kill the creative vibe?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The question stands alone as text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Puts the tension as a direct question.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the central tension of the section.

storyboard.claim: The authors address the tension by pointing to specific organizational research.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a pointer to research.
storyboard.addedInformation: Says the answer comes from the research.

image.subject: a whiteboard covered with colored sticky notes and rough marker sketches, a single hand-drawn lightbulb in the corner

storyboard.claim: In ideation-heavy environments, flat structures foster more creativity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard covered with sticky notes and a lightbulb.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the study's finding.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sticky notes show many ideas kept on the board.

image.subject: an empty theater stage in front of a dark auditorium, a single spotlight on a bare wooden table, the rows of seats fading into shadow

storyboard.claim: Creative work like writing a Broadway show or brainstorming a product category needs flat structures.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty stage with a spotlight on a bare table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives examples of the creative work from the study.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stage stands for the creative process.

left.label: FLAT TEAM
left.subject: a whiteboard covered in colored sticky notes, every note still on the wall, the ideas spread across the board

right.label: TOP-DOWN
right.subject: a whiteboard with a single marker hovering over it and most of the sticky notes torn down, only a few left

storyboard.claim: Flat structures foster creativity because nobody shoots the bad ideas down too early.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two whiteboards: many ideas kept on one, most torn down on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the study's point about creative environments.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the difference in which ideas survive.
